---
title: Modern R and Public Health
---

Public health work is converging on R. This chapter gets your workspace ready so chapter 1 can start with code.

## Why R

If your agency runs SAS, you already know the core loop: read data in, reshape it, summarize it, output it. R does the same thing. The difference is everything around that loop.

**Free.** No license. No seat-count negotiation with procurement. No renewal cycle. R runs on a laptop, a server, or a cloud VM — same tool, same code.

**Analysis lives in a script.** Every step is recorded. Six months later you run the same file and get the same answer. When the Commissioner asks "where did this number come from," you show the code.

**Reports update themselves.** Quarto — the tool this book is built with — embeds code directly in a document. Change a number upstream and the table in the PDF changes with it. No more copy-pasting from Excel into Word.

**The public health ecosystem is here.** CDC, state health departments, and academic epi groups publish R code. Reading it — and writing it — is a basic competency the field is converging on.

**The tidyverse maps to what you already know.** SAS DATA steps and PROC steps have direct equivalents:

| SAS | R (tidyverse) |
|-----|---------------|
| `DATA step` with `WHERE` | `filter()` |
| New variable in `DATA step` | `mutate()` |
| `PROC MEANS` / `PROC FREQ` | `summarise()` + `count()` |
| `BY` statement | `group_by()` |
| `PROC SORT` | `arrange()` |

Syntax changes. Mental model mostly doesn't.

## How this works

Every chapter builds on one analysis: a COVID-19 briefing for a Connecticut health commissioner. You start with a raw CSV and an empty folder. Chapter by chapter the analysis gains new capabilities — until at the end you have a self-updating report that anyone on your team could run.

Each chapter introduces exactly one new skill. The skill earns its place by solving a real problem in the analysis — not as an exercise, but as a genuine improvement to what you built before.

Code along. Every code block in this book is meant to be run, not just read. Open R before you start each chapter and keep it open.

One thing to know about R before you start: unlike SAS, R is interactive. When you run code, results appear immediately in your session. Objects — datasets, plots, numbers — live in memory and you can inspect them at any time. Think of it less like submitting a batch job and more like a conversation with your data.

## The arc

| Part | What you build | The new skill |
|--------|---------------|---------------|
| **Orientation** | Your project folder + first rendered analysis | R mindset; the SAS→R Rosetta stone |
| **Working with Real Data** | A clean, tidy, analysis-ready dataset | `readr`; `janitor`, `tidyr`, `stringr`, `lubridate`, `glue` |
| **Data Visualization** | Trend charts + a CT choropleth, static and interactive | `ggplot2`; `sf` + `tigris`; `leaflet`/`mapview` |
| **Checkpoint** | A one-paragraph status report, built from everything so far | Nothing new — just pulling the pieces together |
| **Managing Code** | A project with real, reviewable history | git: commits, history, branches |
| **Intermediate R** | One template that works for any town | Functions; the state's open-data API |
| **Security Basics** | Credentials that never live in your script | Environment variables; `keyring` |

Further Reading picks up deeper dives — joins, Excel files, writing data
out — whenever a chapter needs one and you want more than the quick
version.

## How to use this site

Work through chapters in order. Each one has:

- **Lesson** (`index.qmd`) — a narrated, runnable walkthrough of the new
  ideas, with code you type out yourself as you read
- **Project** (`project.qmd`) — on the main arc chapters, a shorter pass
  that puts the lesson to work on the running COVID briefing and leaves
  something real in your `covid-briefing/` folder

Read the lesson first, then do the project. The project picks up where
the last one left off, so skipping one will leave you missing a file the
next one expects.

## Before you start

You need three pieces of software before chapter 1: **R** itself, an
**IDE** to write R in (RStudio or Positron), and **Quarto** to build the
report. The rest of this section walks through each one.

::: {.callout-important}
## Check with your IT department first

On a government-managed machine you often cannot install software
yourself, and the steps below may not apply. Many agencies push R,
RStudio, and Positron through a software center, a managed installer, or
a locked-down internal package mirror instead of the public download
sites.

Always defer to your IT or security team on **what** to install, **how**
to install it, and **where** packages are allowed to come from. Treat the
links here as a description of the pieces you need — not as permission to
bypass agency policy. When in doubt, send IT this list and ask them how
your agency does it.
:::

### Step 1 — Install R

R is the language and the engine that runs your code. Everything else
sits on top of it.

- Download it from [r-project.org](https://www.r-project.org) → CRAN →
  pick a mirror → choose your operating system (Windows, macOS, or Linux).
- Get version **4.3 or newer**.
- Accept the defaults during install unless IT tells you otherwise.

R by itself is just the engine — you rarely open it directly. You drive
it through an IDE, which is Step 2.

### Step 2 — Install an IDE (RStudio *or* Positron)

An **IDE** (Integrated Development Environment) is the program you
actually sit in front of: a code editor, a live R console, your plots,
your files, and your data all in one window. You only need **one** of the
two below — either works for everything in this book.

**RStudio** is the long-standing standard for R. If you have ever seen a
screenshot of someone using R, it was almost certainly RStudio. It is
mature, stable, and what most R tutorials and colleagues assume.

- Download: [posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop](https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/)
- Install R (Step 1) **first** — RStudio finds it automatically.

**Positron** is a newer IDE from the same company (Posit). It is built on
the same foundation as VS Code and handles **R and Python side by side**,
which is handy if your team works in both.

- Download: [positron.posit.co](https://positron.posit.co/)
- Also needs R (Step 1) installed first.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Which one should you pick?

If you are brand new, or your colleagues already use RStudio, choose
**RStudio** — you will have more people to ask for help. If you also work
in Python, or want the newer VS Code-style experience, choose
**Positron**. This book's instructions work in both, and you can switch
later.
:::

### Step 3 — Install Quarto

Quarto turns your code and writing into a finished report — HTML, PDF, or
Word. It is what builds the COVID briefing at the end of this book.

- Download: [quarto.org/docs/get-started](https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/)
- Recent versions of RStudio ship Quarto bundled in, so you may already
  have it. Installing it separately does no harm.

### A note on packages and CRAN

Base R can already do a great deal, but its real power comes from
**packages** — bundles of extra functions someone else has written,
tested, and documented so you don't have to. Think of base R as a stocked
kitchen and packages as specialized appliances: `readr` reads data files,
`dplyr` reshapes tables, `ggplot2` draws charts. This book leans heavily
on a family of packages called the **tidyverse**.

Where do packages come from? Mostly **CRAN** — the *Comprehensive R
Archive Network*. CRAN is R's official, curated package repository (the
same network you downloaded R itself from). Every package on CRAN is
checked to install and run on the major operating systems before it is
accepted, which makes it a trustworthy default source.

R ships with a built-in installer, `install.packages()`. It works, and
you'll see it everywhere in older tutorials — but this book uses a more
modern tool called **`pak`** instead. `pak` is itself a package, so you
install it *once* with the built-in installer, and after that you let
`pak` do the rest:

```r
# One time, to get pak itself (the one place we use install.packages):
install.packages("pak")
```

From then on, install anything with `pak::pak()`:

```r
pak::pak("readr")
```

Notice the `pak::pak()` form — `package::function()`. The `::` reaches
into a package and uses one function from it *without* loading the whole
package with `library()`. It's a common R idiom, and it's why you never
have to `library(pak)`.

Why `pak` over the built-in `install.packages()`? It's faster (it
downloads in parallel), it sorts out dependencies and system libraries
more cleanly, it gives clearer error messages, and the *same* function
installs from CRAN, GitHub, or Bioconductor — one command instead of
three.

Once a package is installed, load it at the top of each script that uses
it with `library()`:

```r
library(readr)
```

**Install once, load every session.** `pak::pak()` downloads the package
to your machine and you rarely run it again. `library()` switches a
package on for the current R session — you call it every time you restart
R. Chapter 1 will have you install the handful of packages the book uses.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Packages and your IT department

Installing a package reaches out to the internet to download from CRAN.
On a locked-down agency network that connection may be blocked, or your
organization may run its **own internal mirror** of CRAN that has been
vetted for security. `pak` honors the same configured repositories as the
built-in installer, so whatever mirror IT sets up, it will use. If an
install fails or hangs, that is usually a network or policy issue, not a
mistake on your end — ask IT where your agency expects packages to come
from.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Later: Posit Public Package Manager (P3M)

There's a hosted service called [Posit Public Package
Manager](https://packagemanager.posit.co/) (P3M) that serves pre-built
packages — installs are faster and you can pin to a snapshot of CRAN from
a specific date, which is gold for reproducibility. We'll wire it up in
the reproducibility material *after* the git chapter, once you have a
project whose history is worth locking down. For now, plain `pak::pak()`
against CRAN is all you need — just file the name away.
:::

## What you'll need

- A computer where you can install software (or IT support to install it
  for you)
- R, an IDE (RStudio or Positron), and Quarto — see the steps above
- An internet connection to download the dataset and packages
- No prior programming experience required

## The scenario

The pandemic is in full swing and you are working as an analyst for
the Connecticut Department of Public Health's Pandemic Incident Command.
You are tasked with preparing a briefing for the Commissioner so that they
can in turn brief the governor on the current situation.

The first standing question is this: **Is it getting worse in Hartford, or not?**

Today we are going to answer that question, click by click. Slowly we will
build up our R knowledge and reduce friction until we have an analysis
we can share with others.

### Folder Structure

It is good practice to stick with a common folder layout for each of your
projects. Different programming languages have different conventions but
many layouts are very similar. This reduces the cognitive load for yourself
and others when navigating larger projects. There are tools for creating,
saving, and sharing project templates, but for now we will do this by hand.

1. Create a new folder called `covid-briefing` wherever you keep projects.
2. Inside it, create these folders one at a time:
   - `data`
   - `R`
   - `scripts`
   - `outputs`
   - `docs`
3. Inside `data`, create two more folders: `raw` and `processed`.
4. Inside `outputs`, create two more folders: `figures` and `tables`.

At the end you should have a folder structure that looks like this:

```
covid-briefing/
├── data/
│   ├── raw/
│   │   └── ct_covid_by_town_2026-06-30.csv   ← you'll add this shortly
│   └── processed/
├── R/
├── scripts/
├── outputs/
│   ├── figures/
│   └── tables/
└── docs/
```

**Why these specific folders?**

| Folder | Purpose | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| `data/raw` | Exactly what you downloaded | Never edit a file in here. |
| `data/processed` | Cleaned data you can trust | Always regenerable from `raw` + a script |
| `R` | Reusable functions | Empty today — used once you stop copy-pasting |
| `scripts` | Numbered analysis steps | `01_`, `02_`, ... so the order is obvious |
| `outputs/figures` | Plots | Never hand-edited; always regenerated |
| `outputs/tables` | Summary CSVs etc... | Same rule as figures |
| `docs` | Reports | Empty today — used when you build the briefing doc |

### Open the Project in Your IDE

Once the folders exist, open the project in RStudio or Positron so that
every path you write in code is relative to `covid-briefing/`, not to
your Desktop or Downloads folder.

**RStudio:** File → New Project → Existing Directory → select `covid-briefing` → Create Project.

**Positron:** File → Open Folder → select `covid-briefing`.

Either way, the IDE will reopen with `covid-briefing` as your working
directory. This matters throughout the rest of the book.

### Getting the Data

1. Go to the Open Data dataset page: [Covid 19 Tests, Cases and Deaths by Town ARCHIVE](https://data.ct.gov/Health-and-Human-Services/COVID-19-Tests-Cases-and-Deaths-By-Town-ARCHIVE/28fr-iqnx/about_data)
2. Click **Export → CSV** to download it.
3. Move the downloaded file into `data/raw/`.
4. Rename it to include the date you downloaded it, e.g.:
   `ct_covid_by_town_2026-06-30.csv`

::: {.callout-tip}
Every dataset this book uses — with its source page and direct download links —
is cataloged in the [Data Library](../data-library/index.qmd) at the end of the
book. If you ever need to find or re-download source data, that's where to look.
:::

The date stamp matters more than it looks like it should. This dataset is
revised after the fact — Connecticut DPH updates prior dates as new reports
come in. Stamping the filename is how you'll later be able to say
"this analysis used the data *as it existed on this date,*" which is
exactly the kind of question a Commissioner will ask you.

From this point forward: **never open this file and edit it by hand.** If
something about it needs to change, that change happens in a script, not in
the file itself.

::: {.callout-note}
Want to check your folder structure against a reference? See
[`project-snapshots/after-ch-00`](https://github.com/CT-DPH-Data-Management-and-Governance/modern-r-for-public-health-practitioners/tree/main/project-snapshots/after-ch-00)
on GitHub for what `covid-briefing/` should look like at this point.
:::

### Diving In

Workspace is ready, data is in `data/raw/`. Next chapter: write your first R code.
